extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor, literary critics, and psychologists of laughter
extracted.subtask_description: A historical and theoretical survey of competing accounts of humor and laughter (Greek philosophers through modern psychologists), extracting the conceptual criteria by which comic experience is characterized and judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity of humor and pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor lies close to pathos; a modulation between serious and playful pain can enhance enjoyment of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good humor can move between seriousness and playfulness — 'a modulation between serious and playful pain' — producing a poignant, tremulous pleasure. Anti-pattern: 'fresh' or flippant jokers destroy pathos; pathos is 'impossible to the flippant' and their presence 'blanches' its color. Example: scenes like Sentimental Tommy where laughter and pity mix ('I did not know whether to laugh or cry').

rubrics_metrics.name: Rich, human positive values in jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that are 'rich and human in their positive values' open an avenue to art and resist mere flippancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor with human warmth and depth can integrate pathos and comedy; such jokes are durable against cynical or flippant undermining. Anti-pattern: thin, 'insipid depredations of the Smart Aleck' lack this quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold character of laughter (satisfaction vs disappointment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations of laughter fall into three classes: those locating cause in disappointment, those in satisfaction, and those in a mixture of satisfaction with disappointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'complete comic experience' often unites two kinds of laughter — elements of both pleasurable satisfaction and disappointing surprise — so a full account should allow mixed causes rather than a single factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction/derision theory (pleasure at others' misfortunes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato's (and Hobbes's) view that comic pleasure derives from seeing other people's humiliation or 'sudden glory' (a feeling of superiority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This account emphasizes egotistic complacence or scorn ('the pleasure of seeing other people humiliated'). It explains some jokes but is criticized as incomplete and morally suspect. Modifications: Cicero's genial version claims in some cases we laugh at ourselves; later theorists temper it by limiting to slight, non-harmful misfortunes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disappointment/surprise theory (deceived expectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle and later writers identify a joke with a deceived expectation: 'we expect to hear one thing and another is said' or 'that is stated which we did not expect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise and suddenness are central; a joke often works because it violates an anticipated sequence. Example: Aristotle's illustrative line that becomes funny by unexpected word order. This theory combines well with satisfaction accounts when unexpected truth is acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture theory (pleasure mixed with pain)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic can be a genuine mixture of pleasure with pain or pity, not merely pleasure relieving pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's intuition (and later commentators) suggests laughter often contains both pleasurable and painful tinctures (e.g., pity plus amusement). A good analysis should allow for composite emotional states rather than reducing to pure joy or pure scorn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotle's comic object: ugliness that is not harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy consists in some defect or ugliness 'which is not painful or destructive'; the ludicrous is a subdivision of the ugly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define comic objects by being inferior or defective in a non-harmful way (e.g., the distorted comic mask). This distinguishes harmless ridicule from cruel or dangerous forms of mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genial humor as self-directed laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero's reconciliation: when laughter arises from deceived expectation 'our mistake makes us laugh at ourselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genial or kindly humor can be accounted for by self-derision; where the laugher recognizes their own error or shared fallibility, laughter becomes companionable rather than hostile. Use this to distinguish genial jokes from vicious derision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise and suddenness as chief comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Renaissance and classical commentators (e.g., Maggi, Castiglione) emphasize suddenness and deceiving expectation as central: 'the chief matter is to deceive opinion'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In producing or evaluating jokes, assess the role of timing, abrupt reversal, and the audience's anticipated outcome. Anti-pattern: predictable or slowly building reversals that lack suddenness may fail to elicit comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agnostic/anti-definition stance about humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Several thinkers (e.g., Croce, Cazamian, James Sully) argue that humor 'escapes science' and resists a single rigorous definition because its variable elements are indeterminate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of over-generalization: expect many legitimate, varied instances of comic experience. Methodologically, one should allow multiple overlapping categories rather than force a single strict definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor accompanies general conditions of play (satisfaction/dissatisfaction with instincts in play)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is an accompaniment of very general conditions — that of satisfaction and that of dissatisfaction when the instincts are in a state of play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret many comic occasions as instances of 'play' among instincts; evaluate humor by whether it arises from playful interplay of drives rather than specific situational triggers alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derision tempered: playful, slight, non-destructive scorn
rubrics_metrics.description: Later theorists (Groos, Ziegler) qualify derision: we laugh at stupidities and misfortunes only when they are slight and inconsequential; the scorn is essentially playful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether derisive humor is acceptable or comic (rather than cruel), assess the severity and consequences of the misfortune targeted; slight, inconsequential targets are more likely to produce playful laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-phase comic process and inward imitation (Zeising/Groos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Zeising's three phases: shock (object seems to be something), counter-shock (recognition of nothingness), and happy sense of superiority; Groos adds 'inward imitation' in the second phase — aesthetic participation in the absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful comic sequence may move the audience through deception, empathetic imitation/participation, and then release. Evaluate jokes by how they guide perception through these stages and whether the spectator temporarily 'enters' the absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teasing/game model and objective vs subjective comic (Schauer)
rubrics_metrics.description: All comic enterprise can be seen as 'teasing' — a game where players take adversarial roles. Schauer divides comic experience into objective-comic (where we triumph) and subjective-comic (where we are triumphed over).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess humor as a form of social play: does it function as teasing with mutual rules allowing both winning and losing roles? Good humor can include both triumph and being the butt of the joke; anti-pattern: 'teasing' that lacks play rules becomes hurtful rather than comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic as recognition of unexpected truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jokes produce laughter because they state 'that is stated which we did not expect, and we acknowledge it to be true' (Isocrates/Aristotle pun example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate witty remarks by their capacity to reveal an unexpected but recognizable truth — the cognitive recognition of truth can be a source of amusement distinct from mere ridicule or surprise.
